Hello. I'll guide you through each move, nice and slowly. Breathe out as you move, and stop if anything hurts.

Thumb touches. Rest your forearms on a table or your lap. Touch your thumb to the tip of each finger in turn, making a soft O each time. Go back and forth along your fingers, slowly. Light touches. There’s no need to press.
Finger walks. Lay your hand flat on a table. Slowly walk your fingers sideways toward your thumb, one at a time. Then walk them back to the start. Keep your palm resting on the table.

Wrist lifts at the table. Rest your forearm on a table with your hand just past the edge, palm down. Slowly lift your hand up, then lower it down. Keep your forearm still on the table. Move only as far as is comfortable.

Soft towel squeeze. Roll a small hand towel into a tube. Hold it in your hand and squeeze gently for a slow count of three. Relax your grip fully, then squeeze again. A gentle squeeze is plenty. Never squeeze hard.
Palm turns. Sit with your elbows bent at your sides. Slowly turn your palms up to face the ceiling. Then slowly turn them down to face the floor. Keep your elbows tucked in at your sides.
Small yes nods. Sit tall and look straight ahead. Slowly lower your chin a little, as if nodding yes. Lift it back to level. Keep the movement small. Don’t tip your head far back.
Shrug and let go. Let your arms rest by your sides. Slowly lift your shoulders up toward your ears. Pause, then let them gently drop and relax. Breathe out as your shoulders drop.

Elbow circles. Rest your fingertips lightly on your shoulders. Slowly draw circles with your elbows. Halfway through, change direction. If your fingertips won’t reach, let your hands rest on your chest.

Arm raises to the front. Sit tall with your arms by your sides, thumbs pointing forward. Slowly raise both arms in front of you, no higher than your shoulders. Lower them slowly. One arm at a time is fine too.

Wall finger climb. Sit or stand side-on to a wall, close enough to touch it. Walk your fingers slowly up the wall as far as is comfortable. Walk them back down. Stop before you feel any pinching in your shoulder.
Seated side reach. Sit tall with both feet flat on the floor. Rest one hand on the chair seat. Raise your other arm and lean gently away from it, reaching up and over. Keep both hips on the chair.

Pelvic rocks. Sit near the front of your chair with your hands on your thighs. Slowly tilt your hips back so your lower back rounds a little. Then tilt them forward so your lower back arches a little. Keep rocking gently. This is a small, slow movement.
Gentle tummy tighten. Sit tall and breathe normally. Gently draw your belly button in toward your spine. Hold lightly for a count of five, then relax. Keep breathing the whole time.

Seated heel slides. Sit tall with your feet flat on the floor. Slowly slide one foot forward along the floor, straightening the knee a little. Slide it back under your chair as far as is comfortable. A sock on a smooth floor makes it easier.

Knees open and close. Sit with your feet and knees together. Slowly let your knees fall apart, keeping your feet on the floor. Bring them gently back together. Go only as wide as feels comfortable for your hips.
Seated knee lift and hold. Sit tall and hold the sides of your chair. Slowly lift one knee a few inches. Hold for a moment, then lower it slowly. Keep your back tall, not leaning back.
Toe lifts and taps. Sit with your heels on the floor. Lift the front of your feet, then tap them down. Keep a slow, steady rhythm. Good to do any time you have been sitting.

Ankle alphabet. Lift one foot slightly off the floor, or rest your heel down. Slowly draw the letters A, B, C in the air with your big toe. Go as far through the alphabet as feels easy. Small letters are fine.

Towel toe scrunch. Place a small towel flat on the floor under your bare feet. Slowly scrunch the towel toward you with your toes. Relax and spread your toes, then scrunch again. If your toes cramp, stop and wiggle them.

Sit to stand. Sit near the front of a sturdy chair that won’t slide, feet flat and hip-width apart. Lean forward a little and press through your feet to stand up slowly. Use the armrests if you need to. Pause, then sit back down slowly and with control. Repeat at an easy pace, resting whenever you like. Using your hands is completely fine. Stop if your knees or hips hurt sharply.

Heel raises at the counter. Stand facing a kitchen counter or the back of a sturdy chair and hold on with both hands. Slowly rise up onto your toes. Pause, then lower your heels slowly. Repeat at an easy pace. Keep holding on the whole time.
Seated heel raises. Sit tall with your feet flat on the floor. Lift both heels, keeping your toes on the floor. Lower slowly and repeat. Press gently through the balls of your feet.

Wall push-ups. Stand an arm's length from a wall with your feet hip-width apart. Place your palms flat on the wall at shoulder height. Slowly bend your elbows to bring your chest toward the wall. Push gently back to the start. Repeat at an easy pace. Stand closer to the wall to make it easier.

Seated palm press. Sit tall and press your palms together in front of your chest. Press gently for a slow count of five, then relax. Repeat until the timer ends. Keep breathing. Don’t hold your breath.

Side-to-side weight shifts. Stand at a counter and hold on with both hands, feet hip-width apart. Slowly shift your weight onto one foot, then over to the other. Keep both feet on the floor. Hold on the whole time.

Side leg lifts at the counter. Stand at a counter and hold on with both hands. Slowly lift one leg out to the side a few inches, keeping your toes pointing forward. Lower it slowly. Stand tall. Don’t lean over to lift higher.
Standing heel curls. Stand at a counter and hold on with both hands. Slowly bend one knee to bring your heel up behind you. Lower it slowly. Keep your knees side by side.

Slow belly breathing. Get comfortable and rest one hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose and feel your belly rise. Breathe out slowly, as if through a straw. There’s no right way. Just slow down a little.

Longer breath out. Breathe in gently for a count of four. Breathe out slowly for a count of six. Let your shoulders drop each time you breathe out. If counting feels like work, just make the breath out a little longer.
Soften and let go. Close your eyes if you like. Notice your jaw, your shoulders and your hands. Each time you breathe out, let one of them soften a little. Rest is part of looking after your joints.

Why gentle movement helps. Joints are made to move. Regular, gentle movement keeps the muscles around them working and can make everyday tasks feel a little easier. Little and often tends to suit stiff joints better than a lot all at once.

A little soreness can be normal. When you start moving more, you may feel some mild soreness. That’s common, and it usually settles as your body gets used to it. Sharp, severe or worsening pain is different. That’s a sign to stop and ease off.

The two-hour check. Notice how your joints feel about two hours after you move. If they feel worse than before you started, do a little less next time: shorter holds, fewer moves, or the Easy day routine. You don’t need to stop moving altogether.

How much should a move feel?. Aim for a gentle pull or light effort, never pain. Think of a scale from 0 (nothing) to 10 (the worst pain you can imagine). From 0 to 3 is fine. At 4 or 5, go gentler or shorter. Above 5, or if pain is sharp or getting worse as you move, stop that move.

Flare days happen. Flares aren’t your fault, and one bad day doesn’t undo your progress. On those days, smaller movements, seated moves, warmth and rest breaks can help you get through. The Easy day routine and the Breathing break are there for exactly this.
Warm up first. Stiff joints often loosen after a few minutes of easy movement. A warm shower, or a warm (not hot) pack for a few minutes before you start, may also help you feel looser.
Missing a day is fine. This app counts your week, not unbroken days. Missing a day, or a few, is part of real life. Whenever you come back, start gently and pick up where you are.
Breathe while you move. It’s easy to hold your breath while you concentrate. Try breathing slowly in through your nose and out through your mouth. A relaxed breath helps your muscles relax too.

Strength matters too. Stretching helps you move, and gentle strength work helps your muscles support your joints. Simple moves like standing up from a chair or heel raises at a counter count. You’ll find them in the Gentle strength routine.
Pacing your day. Spread bigger jobs across the day and the week. Break a large task into smaller pieces, with rests in between. Stopping before you are worn out often lets you do more across the day.
Sleep and stiff joints. Poor sleep can make pain feel louder, and pain can make sleep harder. A regular bedtime, a calm wind-down and the Evening ease routine may help you settle.
Walking counts. Short, easy walks are good for your whole body. Start with what feels comfortable, even a few minutes, and build slowly. Supportive shoes and level paths make it easier.
Be kind to your hands. Tools with bigger handles, jar openers and lifting with two hands can take strain off sore fingers and wrists. Small changes to how you do everyday jobs add up.
Notice what helps. The Progress page shows the days you moved and how your joints felt. Over a few weeks, you may start to notice patterns, like which routines or times of day suit you best.

Mood and pain are linked. Living with pain can wear you down, and feeling low can make pain harder to cope with. Gentle activity, time outdoors and talking with people you trust can all help. If low mood lasts, please talk to your doctor.
Talking with your doctor. The Progress page has a one-page summary of your sessions and how your joints have felt. You can print it or show it on your phone at your next appointment.
Medicines and movement. Keep taking anything you have been prescribed. Only change or reduce a medicine after speaking with your doctor. Gentle movement works alongside your care, not instead of it.
Cold weather and stiffness. Many people feel stiffer when it’s cold or damp. Warm layers, gloves and a few extra minutes of warm-up can make those days easier.
Celebrate small wins. Opening a jar more easily or getting up from a chair with less effort is real progress. Take a moment to notice it.

Steady on your feet. For any standing move, hold a sturdy counter or chair back. Clear the floor around you, wear non-slip shoes and make sure the room is well lit. You can switch on "Seated only" at any time.

When to get help. Most aches settle with rest and gentle movement. Some signs need a doctor quickly, like a joint that’s suddenly hot, red and swollen, or not being able to put weight on a leg. The full list is on the "When to stop" page.
